name: Rapidity from Velocity
description: Computes the relativistic rapidity from the velocity ratio beta = v/c, as half the natural log of (1+beta) over (1-beta). Rapidity is the additive measure of velocity in special relativity that grows without bound as beta approaches 1.
notes: Beta is dimensionless and must satisfy -1 < beta < 1, or the logarithm is undefined. Unlike velocities, rapidities add linearly under collinear Lorentz boosts, which is their main advantage.

name: Relativistic Aberration of Light
description: Computes the observed direction of a light ray in a frame moving at beta relative to the source, giving the aberrated angle from the emission angle theta. Relativistic motion shifts light forward, concentrating it toward the direction of travel.
notes: Angles are in radians and beta is dimensionless with magnitude below 1. This is the relativistic aberration formula; at beta near 1 most light appears strongly beamed into a narrow forward cone.

name: Transverse Doppler Effect
description: Computes the observed frequency of a source moving transversely to the line of sight, as the source frequency times sqrt(1 - beta^2). It is a purely relativistic redshift caused by time dilation, with no classical counterpart.
notes: Beta is dimensionless with magnitude below 1; output frequency shares the input unit (Hz). This applies at the instant of closest approach where motion is exactly transverse; any radial component adds a classical Doppler shift.

name: Relativistic Doppler Effect (General Angle)
description: Computes the observed frequency for a source moving at beta and viewed at angle theta, combining the classical Doppler shift with relativistic time dilation. It reduces to the transverse effect at theta = pi/2 and the longitudinal effect along the line of motion.
notes: Theta is the observation angle in radians in the observer frame and beta is dimensionless below 1. Sign conventions for theta and beta determine whether the result is a blueshift or redshift, so check the geometry carefully.

name: Invariant Mass from Four-Momentum
description: Computes the invariant (rest) mass of a system from its total energy and momentum, as sqrt(Etot^2/c^4 - p^2/c^2). This Lorentz-invariant combination is the same in every reference frame.
notes: Energy in joules, momentum in kg*m/s, c in m/s give mass in kilograms. The quantity under the root must be non-negative; a negative value indicates inconsistent inputs rather than a physical mass.

name: Relativistic Momentum from Energy
description: Computes the relativistic momentum of a particle from its total energy and rest mass, as sqrt(Etot^2 - (m*c^2)^2) divided by c. It inverts the energy-momentum relation to recover momentum from the energy.
notes: Energy in joules, mass in kilograms, c in m/s give momentum in kg*m/s. Total energy must be at least the rest energy m*c^2, otherwise the square root has no real value.

name: Relativistic Energy (Momentum Form)
description: Computes the total relativistic energy of a particle from its momentum and rest mass, as sqrt((p*c)^2 + (m*c^2)^2). This is the energy-momentum relation combining kinetic and rest energy.
notes: Momentum in kg*m/s, mass in kilograms, c in m/s give energy in joules. For a massless particle it reduces to E = p*c; for zero momentum it gives the rest energy m*c^2.

name: Relativistic Doppler Shift (Wavelength, Receding)
description: Computes the observed wavelength from a source receding along the line of sight, as the rest wavelength times sqrt((1+beta)/(1-beta)). Recession stretches the wavelength, producing a redshift.
notes: Beta is dimensionless with magnitude below 1; output wavelength shares the input unit. This is the longitudinal (radial) receding form; motion at an angle requires the general-angle Doppler formula instead.

name: Relativistic Doppler Shift (Wavelength, Approaching)
description: Computes the observed wavelength from a source approaching along the line of sight, as the rest wavelength times sqrt((1-beta)/(1+beta)). Approach compresses the wavelength, producing a blueshift.
notes: Beta is dimensionless with magnitude below 1; output wavelength shares the input unit. This is the longitudinal approaching form; it is the reciprocal of the receding case for the same beta.

name: Gravitational Redshift (Schwarzschild)
description: Computes the gravitational redshift of light escaping from radius r around a mass M in the Schwarzschild metric, as 1/sqrt(1 - 2GM/(rc^2)) minus 1. It gives the fractional increase in wavelength seen far from the mass.
notes: Radius r must exceed the Schwarzschild radius 2GM/c^2 or the expression is imaginary. The result is the dimensionless redshift z; it diverges as r approaches the event horizon.

name: Schwarzschild Time Dilation Factor
description: Computes the gravitational time dilation factor at radius r around a mass M, as sqrt(1 - 2GM/(rc^2)). It is the ratio of proper time at r to coordinate time far away; clocks deeper in the gravity well run slower.
notes: Radius r must exceed the Schwarzschild radius 2GM/c^2 or the root is imaginary. The dimensionless factor approaches 1 far from the mass and drops to 0 at the event horizon.

name: Escape Velocity (Schwarzschild)
description: Computes the escape velocity from a spherical mass M at radius r, as sqrt(2GM/r), the speed needed to break free of its gravity. When this equals the speed of light, r is the Schwarzschild radius.
notes: SI units (G in N*m^2/kg^2, M in kg, r in m) give the result in m/s. This is the classical Newtonian escape speed; it coincidentally matches the Schwarzschild horizon condition but is not a relativistic derivation.

name: Photon Sphere Radius
description: Computes the radius of the photon sphere around a non-rotating black hole of mass M, as 3GM/c^2. At this radius light can orbit in an unstable circular path, equal to 1.5 times the Schwarzschild radius.
notes: SI units (G, M in kg, c in m/s) give the radius in meters. Valid for a Schwarzschild (non-rotating, uncharged) black hole; rotating Kerr black holes have direction-dependent photon orbits.

name: ISCO Radius (Schwarzschild)
description: Computes the radius of the innermost stable circular orbit around a Schwarzschild black hole of mass M, as 6GM/c^2. Inside this radius no stable circular orbit exists, so orbiting matter spirals inward.
notes: SI units (G, M in kg, c in m/s) give the radius in meters, equal to three Schwarzschild radii. Valid for a non-rotating black hole; spin shifts the ISCO inward for prograde and outward for retrograde orbits.

name: Gravitational Deflection of Light
description: Computes the general-relativistic deflection angle of a light ray grazing a mass M at impact parameter b, as 4GM/(bc^2). This is twice the Newtonian prediction and was confirmed by starlight bending near the Sun.
notes: SI units give the deflection in radians and it assumes a small angle with b well outside the Schwarzschild radius. The impact parameter b is the perpendicular distance of the undeflected ray from the mass center.

name: Shapiro Time Delay
description: Computes the extra light-travel time a signal accumulates when it passes close to a massive body, whose gravity warps spacetime. The delay grows with the deflector mass M and shrinks for larger impact parameter b, giving seconds of added round-trip time in the weak field.
notes: A weak-field, logarithmic approximation valid when the impact parameter b is much larger than the Schwarzschild radius. Distances d1 and d2 are measured from the deflector to source and observer along the line of sight.

name: Relativistic Perihelion Precession
description: Gives the general-relativistic advance of an orbit's perihelion per revolution, in radians. The precession increases with central mass M and orbital eccentricity, and decreases with the semi-major axis a, explaining Mercury's anomalous 43 arcsec-per-century drift.
notes: Result is radians accumulated each orbit; multiply by the number of orbits per century to compare with observed rates. Valid in the weak field for a nearly Keplerian orbit.

name: Chirp Mass (Gravitational Waves)
description: Combines the two component masses of an inspiraling binary into the single chirp mass that controls how fast its gravitational-wave frequency sweeps upward. It weights the product and sum of m1 and m2 so that this one number governs the observed waveform.
notes: Inputs and result share the same mass unit (kg here); the value is symmetric in m1 and m2. It sets the leading-order inspiral rate but does not by itself give the individual masses.

name: Gravitational Wave Luminosity (Quadrupole)
description: Estimates the power radiated as gravitational waves by two point masses in a circular orbit, using the quadrupole formula. The output in watts rises steeply with the masses and falls as the fifth power of their separation r, so it dominates only in tight, massive binaries.
notes: Assumes a Newtonian circular orbit and point masses; it is an order-of-magnitude approximation that breaks down near merger. Extremely sensitive to r through the 1/r^5 factor.

name: Schwarzschild Surface Gravity
description: Gives the surface gravity of a non-rotating black hole at its event horizon as c^4/(4GM). The value in m/s squared is inversely proportional to mass, so larger black holes have weaker horizon gravity.
notes: This is the standard surface gravity kappa (as an acceleration), not the tidal force felt by an infalling observer. It applies to the Schwarzschild horizon only, with no spin or charge.

name: Hawking Temperature
description: Computes the temperature of the thermal radiation a Schwarzschild black hole emits from quantum effects at its horizon. The temperature in kelvin is inversely proportional to mass M, so a solar-mass black hole is fantastically cold, far below the CMB.
notes: Applies to a non-rotating, uncharged black hole. Larger black holes are colder; the tiny values make astrophysical black holes effectively non-evaporating today.

name: Black Hole Evaporation Time
description: Estimates how long a Schwarzschild black hole takes to fully evaporate via Hawking radiation, in seconds. The lifetime scales as the cube of the mass M, so heavier black holes last vastly longer while tiny ones vanish quickly.
notes: Assumes only Hawking emission with no infalling matter and ignores CMB heating, which would prevent evaporation of stellar-mass holes today. Strongly sensitive to M through the M^3 factor.

name: Kretschmann Scalar (Schwarzschild)
description: Gives the Kretschmann curvature scalar of the Schwarzschild geometry, a coordinate-independent measure of spacetime curvature. In units of 1/m^4 it grows as 1/r^6, diverging at the central singularity and staying finite and smooth at the horizon.
notes: The finite value at the event horizon shows the horizon is a coordinate artifact, not a true singularity; only r=0 is a genuine curvature singularity. Radius r is the areal radial coordinate.

name: Relativistic Larmor Power
description: Computes the power radiated by an accelerating charge at relativistic speeds for acceleration parallel to velocity, in watts. It generalizes the Larmor formula with a gamma^6 factor, so radiation grows enormously as the Lorentz factor increases.
notes: The gamma^6 scaling holds for linear (parallel) acceleration; perpendicular acceleration carries a gamma^4 factor instead. Here a is the proper acceleration and q the particle charge.

name: Thomas Precession Rate
description: Gives the rate at which a moving particle's spin axis precesses purely from special-relativistic velocity composition, in radians per second. It depends on the Lorentz factor and on acceleration perpendicular to velocity, and vanishes when the two are parallel.
notes: This is the magnitude for acceleration perpendicular to velocity; a and v should be the perpendicular components. It is a kinematic effect distinct from any torque on the spin.

name: Relativistic Cyclotron Frequency
description: Computes the angular gyration frequency of a charged particle in a magnetic field once its relativistic mass increase is included, as qB/(gamma m). The frequency in rad/s drops as the Lorentz factor gamma rises, so fast particles orbit more slowly.
notes: Divide by 2*pi to get the frequency in Hz. The gamma factor reduces the non-relativistic cyclotron frequency; m is the rest mass and B the field magnitude.

name: Bondi k-Factor
description: Computes the relativistic Doppler k-factor sqrt((1+beta)/(1-beta)), the ratio by which signal intervals stretch or compress between observers in relative motion. Values above one indicate recession (redshift) and below one indicate approach.
notes: The input beta is the speed as a fraction of c and must satisfy -1 < beta < 1. This longitudinal factor equals the relativistic Doppler shift ratio in Bondi's k-calculus.

name: Gravitational Redshift (Weak Field)
description: Computes the fractional shift in a photon's frequency as it climbs a height h in a weak, uniform gravitational field, as gh/c^2. The dimensionless result gives how much light is redshifted going up (or blueshifted going down).
notes: A weak-field approximation valid when gh is much smaller than c^2. The result is the fractional shift delta_f/f, not a frequency; multiply by the base frequency to get the actual shift.

name: Sagnac Effect Time Difference
description: Gives the arrival-time difference between two light beams traveling in opposite directions around a rotating loop, as 4*A*omega/c^2. The result in seconds is proportional to the enclosed area A and the angular velocity, and underlies ring-laser and fiber-optic gyroscopes.
notes: A is the area enclosed by the loop and omega its rotation rate; the effect is independent of the loop shape. The default omega matches Earth's rotation. The value is a tiny time difference.

name: Relativistic Momentum (Rapidity Form)
description: Computes a particle's relativistic momentum expressed through rapidity, as m*c*sinh(phi). Because the hyperbolic sine of rapidity equals gamma*beta, this reproduces the usual momentum while adding rapidities linearly instead of velocities.
notes: The bracket (exp(phi) - exp(-phi))/2 is sinh(phi); rapidity phi is dimensionless and additive under boosts. Result is in kg*m/s for mass in kg.

name: Relativistic Energy (Rapidity Form)
description: Gives a particle's total relativistic energy in terms of rapidity, as m*c^2*cosh(phi). Since the hyperbolic cosine of rapidity equals the Lorentz factor gamma, this equals gamma*m*c^2 and reduces to the rest energy when the rapidity is zero.
notes: The bracket (exp(phi) + exp(-phi))/2 is cosh(phi), which equals gamma. Result is in joules for mass in kg; at phi=0 it returns the rest energy m*c^2.

name: Unruh Temperature
description: Computes the temperature of the thermal bath a uniformly accelerating observer perceives in vacuum, as hbar*a/(2*pi*c*kB). The temperature in kelvin is proportional to the proper acceleration a, linking acceleration to an apparent thermal glow.
notes: Input a is the proper acceleration; even 1e20 m/s^2 gives only a fraction of a kelvin, so the effect is minuscule at everyday accelerations. It is the accelerated-frame analog of Hawking temperature.

name: Gravitational Wave Strain (Order Estimate)
description: Provides an order-of-magnitude estimate of the gravitational-wave strain at distance r from a source, as 4*G*Ekin/(c^4*r). The dimensionless strain scales with the non-spherical kinetic energy Ekin and falls off as 1/r.
notes: A rough scaling estimate, not a precise waveform; only the non-spherically-symmetric part of the kinetic energy radiates. Result is the fractional length change h, typically around 1e-21 at Earth.

name: Geodetic Precession Rate
description: Gives the geodetic (de Sitter) precession rate of a gyroscope orbiting a mass, as 3*G*M*v/(2*c^2*r^2). This general-relativistic effect in rad/s arises from parallel transport of the spin through curved spacetime and was confirmed by Gravity Probe B.
notes: A weak-field expression; here v is the orbital velocity and r the orbital radius. It is distinct from frame-dragging (Lense-Thirring), which depends on the central body's spin.

name: Lense-Thirring Precession
description: Computes the frame-dragging precession rate caused by a rotating mass's angular momentum J, as 2*G*J/(c^2*r^3). The result in rad/s shows how a spinning body twists nearby spacetime, precessing gyroscopes and orbits.
notes: A weak-field expression that falls off as 1/r^3; J is the central body's angular momentum. This is distinct from geodetic precession, which arises from the body's mass rather than its spin.

name: Kerr Outer Horizon Radius
description: Gives the outer event-horizon radius of a rotating (Kerr) black hole, as G*M*(1 + sqrt(1 - astar^2))/c^2. Increasing the dimensionless spin astar shrinks the horizon from the Schwarzschild value toward half of it at maximal spin.
notes: The dimensionless spin astar must satisfy |astar| <= 1, or the square root becomes imaginary and no horizon exists (a naked singularity). At astar=0 it returns the Schwarzschild radius.

name: Relativistic Rocket Velocity
description: Computes the velocity of a rocket undergoing constant proper acceleration a, as c*tanh(a*t/c) in coordinate time t. The speed rises linearly at first but saturates just below the speed of light no matter how long the burn continues.
notes: The expression equals c*tanh(a*t/c); t is coordinate (Earth-frame) time, not the traveler's proper time. Result stays strictly below c. Default a is one Earth gravity.

name: Relativistic Rocket Distance
description: Gives the distance covered by a rocket under constant proper acceleration a, as (c^2/a)*(cosh(a*t/c) - 1) in coordinate time t. For long times the distance grows almost linearly (near light speed) after an early quadratic phase.
notes: The bracket equals cosh(a*t/c) - 1; t is coordinate time measured in the launch frame. Distance is in meters for SI inputs. Default a is one Earth gravity.

name: Relativistic Rocket Proper Time
description: Computes the proper time experienced aboard a rocket with constant proper acceleration a after a given coordinate time t, as (c/a)*arcsinh(a*t/c). It grows only logarithmically for large t, so the crew ages far less than mission clocks on Earth.
notes: The logarithm term equals arcsinh(a*t/c); t is the coordinate (Earth-frame) time and the result is the shipboard elapsed time. Default a is one Earth gravity.

name: Center-of-Mass Energy (Fixed Target)
description: Estimates the center-of-mass collision energy in a fixed-target experiment, as sqrt(2*m*c^2*Eb) for beam energy Eb striking a stationary mass m. It grows only as the square root of beam energy, which is why colliders outperform fixed targets.
notes: A high-energy approximation valid when the beam energy Eb greatly exceeds the target rest energy m*c^2. Eb is the beam's total energy; result is in joules for SI inputs.

name: Relativistic Speed from Kinetic Energy
description: Recovers a particle's speed as a fraction of c from its kinetic energy, as sqrt(1 - 1/(1 + KE/(m*c^2))^2). The result beta approaches 1 as the kinetic energy grows far beyond the rest energy m*c^2.
notes: Result is the dimensionless ratio beta = v/c, not a velocity; multiply by c for m/s. KE is kinetic energy and m the rest mass. Valid for any positive KE.

name: Lorentz Factor from Kinetic Energy
description: Gives the Lorentz factor gamma of a particle directly from its kinetic energy, as 1 + KE/(m*c^2). Since total energy is gamma*m*c^2 and kinetic energy is the excess over rest energy, the ratio KE/(m*c^2) simply adds to one.
notes: The dimensionless result is at least 1; it equals 1 when KE is zero (particle at rest). KE is kinetic energy and m the rest mass, in consistent SI units.

name: GPS Relativistic Frequency Shift
description: Estimates the fractional frequency difference between a GPS satellite clock and one on Earth's surface, combining gravitational blueshift with the satellite's time-dilation term. The gravitational part speeds the orbiting clock while its motion slows it, netting a small positive shift.
notes: A weak-field approximation; the result is a dimensionless fractional rate that must be corrected for GPS to work. Uses potential difference between surface radius rE and orbit radius rsat plus the velocity term.
